name: Summit Peaks Resorts
blurb: Public ski company, six mountains, one season pass. Founder Dana Strand built it from a single hill in Alder Creek and holds 30% of the vote. Alder Creek is the oldest mountain and the town's main employer.

directors.name: Marisa Kell
directors.title: Attorney
directors.motive: You have held the engineer's full warning for a week. It says the grip fails only under sustained cold below minus 10 C, true at just three of the 41 lifts, and nobody else has read that. Releasing it risks the CEO's trust, and holding it risks your seat.

directors.name: Tomas Reyes
directors.title: Labor director
directors.motive: Your union builds and runs the lifts, and an operator died Sunday. A full shutdown means layoffs, and your pension sits in the fund they would hit. You want the dangerous lifts shut and the safe ones working, not a blanket closure.

directors.name: Grace Whitlow
directors.title: Fund partner
directors.motive: Your fund owns 8% and your bonus depends on a share price the buybacks support. A full stop drops the stock, and regulators punish stalling. You would rather let regulators set the timetable and keep the lifts open until they do.

directors.name: Hal Brennan
directors.title: Founder's friend
directors.motive: Dana Strand is your college roommate and believes the CEO. She put you on this board and does not want a leadership fight. Splitting the roles would read as a verdict on her pick, so you would carry her view and keep the lifts open.

directors.name: June Okafor
directors.title: Community seat
directors.motive: You are Mayor of Alder Creek and went to two funerals. The town lives on Summit's jobs and taxes, and you face re-election in the fall. A three-week committee keeps paychecks while showing the town someone is looking, so you favor it.

directors.name: Ines Calder
directors.title: Audit chair
directors.motive: You led the risk review that rated lift risk low. A full stop brings an outside review that reads your work first, and a new safety committee would too. You prefer the regulators set the pace, and you would not volunteer for either.

briefing.intro: Summit Peaks runs six ski mountains on one season pass and its most profitable product is the Series 7 gondola, a lift it also builds and sells to other resorts. The board has no safety committee, and founder Dana Strand holds 30% of the vote.
facts: Two Series 7 cabins have fallen from their cables in five months. The first killed 18 riders at a partner resort, and the second, last Sunday at Summit's Alder Creek mountain, killed 12 riders and a lift operator. Regulators have closed the model elsewhere but not yet Summit's 41 lifts.

A software fix has slipped three times and could be ready in about eleven weeks, with approval not before August. The cable grip reads a single sensor, and an engineer warned two years ago the design was undertested. The board never saw the message.

The Series 7 brings in $2.1 billion of $9 billion in revenue. Stopping would cost about $1 billion in supplier payments and thousands of jobs, while running on risks criminal claims, a lost license and voided insurance. Nobody inside can say which risk is larger.

The CEO, who is also Chair, believes the lift is sound and says a recall sends the wrong signal. The stock is $380, down 12%, and Summit spends $4 billion a year on dividends and buybacks. A congressional committee wants documents by April 15.

options.title: Stop all Series 7 lifts
options.text: Close every Series 7 lift and halt production for an outside safety review; about $1 billion in supplier payments and thousands of jobs are at risk.

options.title: Close Alder Creek only
options.text: Close Alder Creek and any lift regulators order closed, and keep building while the fix is finished; families' lawyers will cite a decision made after two falls.

options.title: Keep running, defend
options.text: Keep every lift open and wait for regulators; a third fall, a license loss or voided insurance could end the company.

options.title: Split Chair and CEO
options.text: Separate the roles and let a new safety committee decide after three weeks; every lift stays open in the meantime.

reveal.text: The real firm was Boeing, after two 737 MAX crashes killed 346 people in 2018 and 2019. Boeing cut production, created a board safety committee only in September 2019, and removed Dennis Muilenburg as Chair in October and as CEO in December. A shareholder suit over ignored safety warnings settled for $237.5 million.

questions: Why would a lift maker rely on a single sensor?
The engineer's warning never reached the board. Who blocked it?
Ground every lift or keep running? Pick one.
Should the CEO also be Chair? Yes or no?

press.headline: Summit Peaks Grounds All Series 7 Lifts
press.story: Summit closed every Series 7 lift and suspended dividends and buybacks pending an independent safety review. Suppliers face about $1 billion in lost orders, thousands of jobs are at risk, and a rival lift maker is already calling Summit's customers.

press.headline: Summit Closes Alder Creek, Keeps Other Series 7 Lifts Running
press.story: The company says its software fix will make the lift safe, with approval not expected before August. Families' lawyers said the decision to keep running after two falls will be central in court.

press.headline: Summit Peaks Defends Its Record as Lifts Keep Running
press.story: Summit left every Series 7 lift open and kept building, so no jobs were cut this week and the stock held up better than feared. Within days the state regulator ordered closures anyway, and insurers said coverage may be void.

press.headline: Summit Peaks Splits Chair and CEO, Forms Safety Committee
press.story: A new board committee can see all engineering messages and will decide on the lifts after three weeks. Investors welcomed the governance change, but every Series 7 lift stays open in the meantime, and one regulator said it will not wait that long.
